Contextualizing Mathematical Problem-Solving Instruction for Secondary Students with Extensive Support Needs: A Systematic Replication
Jenny R. Root, Sarah K. Cox, Kat Davis, Nanette Hammons

Abstract
Replication research provides evidence to establish, refute, or support evidence-based practices. Systematic replications are also necessary to determine “what works for whom when.” The purpose of this study was to conduct a conceptual systematic replication to evaluate the effectiveness of a multicomponent treatment package on multiplicative problem solving for middle school students with extensive support needs. Using a modified schema-based instructional strategy, three participants were taught to solve percent of change problems contextualized in real-world scenarios and a purchasing strategy (i.e., next-dollar strategy) to help them determine how much money was needed to pay for services/products. decision.reason: Apply Step2 identification by description to the specific reported finding, not to every component antecedent. Current abstract describes a multicomponent package combining MSBIpercent-of-change word problems, real-world contexts and goal/self-graphing in three secondary students, with a functional relation and coupon/receipt generalization. The independently verified2018Root original at133positively reports this compound finding. The2017personal-finance addition/subtraction and Browder2018component/method studies do not positively report that same compound percent-change/goal-graphing finding. Their presence does not make the uniquely fitting report ambiguous, and a current-body citation is not mandatory when description plus complete bibliography and primary original content uniquely identify an entry. Bind existing133by description. This does not exclude unseen separately tested component findings or infer independent participants from dates, and it creates no extra pair.

Mixed-Reality Simulation With Preservice Teacher Candidates: A Conceptual Replication
Walters, Sharon M.; Hirsch, Shanna E.; McKown, Georgia; Carlson, Alex; Allen, Abigail A.
DOI: 10.1177/08884064211001453

Abstract
Given the critical importance of discrete instructional practices in special education, teacher candidates must be prepared to implement them upon entering the classroom. In preservice teacher education programs, field placements and clinical experiences rarely provide enough opportunities for preservice teachers to gain the proficiency needed to provide effective instruction. In this study, a randomized control research design was used to investigate the effects of a mixed-reality simulation experience compared with traditional classroom practice in the implementation of a system of least prompts. Results suggest that mixed-reality simulation with additional coaching supports significantly improved preservice teachers’ implementation of the prompting sequence. decision.reason: The complete deposited references include one positively matching empirical finding: VinceGarland etal individual clinical coaching in TLETeachLivE improves novice teachers system-of-least-prompts implementation fidelity. Its primary original abstract reports six novice educators and this specific training/skill result; the current conceptual-replication title and abstract test coached mixed-reality SLPimplementation against classroom practice. Other simulation/teacher-education/reading-comprehension/bullying references do not positively report that same joint SLPcoaching/fidelity finding. Step2 permits naming this unique entry by description without an explicit in-text citation in the available abstract. Bind existing145, preserving verified2015online/2016print identity as one work. No full protocol equivalence, exact replication, hidden current comparisons or outcome is inferred.

decision.quote:
Neonatal imitation: Two failures to replicate
Jean E. Koepke, Marilyn Hamm, Maria Legerstee, Mary Russell
Abstract
The purpose of the present research was to replicate two experiments in which neonatal imitation was reported. In replicating the first experiment tongue- and lip-protrusion, mouth-opening, and sequential finger movement were modeled for six 2-week-old babies. Judgments of which models the babies were probably watching and trying to imitate were made from video-tape records of their behavior. In replicating the second experiment mouth-opening and tongue-protrusion were modeled for 14 babies 17- to 21-days-old. Videotape records of their behavior were scored for frequency of imitative behaviors. In replicating the first experiment a potential for experimenter bias that was inherent in the procedure was eliminated and in replicating the second the reliability of the scoring procedure, limited to within scorer originally, was extended to include between scorer as well. The results of both replications failed to yield evidence of neonatal imitation and thus raise questions a
decision.reason: The recovered complete1977Science article at319positively supplies both source-described experiments: first the four facial/manual gesture models in six neonates and video judgments, second mouth-opening/tongue-protrusion frequency scoring with within-observer reliability. Current abstract independently describes those two experiments and specific bias/reliability extensions. This compound procedural/finding fingerprint, the exact published citation and full primary original establish the unique positively fitting report under Step2description rule. Jacobson1979primary evidence concerns older infants and different stimuli. UnrecoveredHayes1981and earlier1975/1976Meltzoffreports do not supply positive evidence of a different equally fitting tested pair; do not demand an impossible exclusion of hypothetical unseen reports or explicit current in-text citation when description is diagnostic. Prefer the complete published1977report over earlier presentation/thesis accounts, without claiming every report/cohort identical. Both experiments are one original paper, not two missing originals. Bind existing319; current-body absence and unrecovered alternate-report details remain recorded, but do not negate this positive identity.
